findings.description: map_public_ip_on_launch = true means every instance launched into this subnet, which routes to the internet gateway via the 0.0.0.0/0 default route, receives a public IP and is reachable from the internet by default.
map_public_ip_on_launch = true on a subnet associated with a route table that has a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the internet gateway, so instances placed here are internet-reachable without explicit intent.
The EBS volume has no encrypted = true (and no kms_key_id), so the attached disk, including anything the portal server writes to /dev/sdh, is stored unencrypted.

The instance's user_data embeds a long-lived AWS access key ID and secret access key in cleartext. User data is stored in instance metadata and readable by any process or user on the instance, and is also visible to anyone with EC2 describe permissions, so these credentials should be considered compromised; they should be replaced with an IAM role/instance profile.

The ingress rule allows TCP/22 from 0.0.0.0/0, exposing SSH administration of the instance to the entire internet and permitting brute-force or credential-stuffing attacks against a host that already carries embedded credentials.
The ingress rule allows TCP/80 from 0.0.0.0/0, publishing the web service to the internet without any source restriction or intermediary load balancer/WAF boundary.
The S3 bucket that receives VPC flow logs has no server-side encryption configuration, so the network traffic metadata it stores is written unencrypted at rest.

Apache serves the instance on port 80 over plain HTTP with no TLS listener or certificate, so content and any traffic to the portal are transmitted in the clear and can be intercepted or modified in transit.
The egress rule permits all protocols and all ports to 0.0.0.0/0, giving a compromised instance unrestricted outbound access for data exfiltration and command-and-control callbacks.
